text.p: These are the leading stories in the Namibian press on Friday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- U.S. president Bill Clinton will make the final decision whether Washington will throw its weight behind a bid by Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe to have their elephant populations downlisted at a crucial CITES conference in Zimbabwe next month. The Clinton administration was closely studying proposals by the three countries. CITES has listed the African elephant under Appendix I of the Convention, which bans trade in ivory and other animal products. The countries are fighting to have their elephant populations downdraded to Appendix II to allow controlled trading.

- Southern African Development Community intra-regional trade and growth has been hampered by impediments like trade barriers, poor infrastructure and policies governing the flow of capital across regional borders. Standard Bank Namibia's managing director, Vic Moll, told last week's World Economic Forum in Zimbabwe that impediments needed to be removed before addressing the issue of monetary harmonisation.

- President Sam Nujoma has rejected a proposal for the establishment of an African peacekeeping force that could be deployed to trouble spots on the continet. At a news conference in New York during his three-day visit to the U.S., Nujoma said the maintenance of inernational peace and security should be the responsibility of the United Nations.

- The chairman of the organisation "Breaking the Wall of Silence" on Monday said the aim of national reconciliation could not be realised if the past was not settled. "We cannot expect the victims to forgive if there is no regret on the part of the perpetrators," BWS chairman Samson Ndeikwila said. He said the ruling Swapo party could hide from the truth, but could not escape it. BWS is fighting to have the ruling party admit human rights violations against people in its own ranks during the war of liberation.

- There is no certainty yet whether President Sam Nujoma will agree to a change of the constitution to allow him to stand for a third term, desite pressure from within Swapo ranks to do so. Even if the Swapo congress, beginning on Wednesday, agrees to a third term, it is still possible that the president will not accept his nomination for the 1999 elections if he is convinced that a suitable successor has been found.

- Amid serious internal division regarding certain leadership positions in Swapo and insecurity about the future, the central committee meets on tuesday morning to put up a list of candidates and an agenda for the congress, which has to be ratified by President Sam Nujoma before Tuesday evening. In what can be described as a watershed congress of the party, there is great interest in the election of a party vice president, who will be accepted as Nujoma's successor for the the party leadership. Vying for the position are Prime Minister Hage Geingob and deputy prime minster Hendrik Witbooi.
